findings.title: Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request context
findings.body: Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine and derive its context with context.WithTimeoutCause on the incoming request context (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163). A child context is cancelled as soon as its parent is cancelled, and the apiserver cancels the request context when the handler returns — which is immediately after these methods return success. The 10s timeout therefore never keeps the legacy call alive; Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection run with an already-cancelled context and fail. Mode 3 reads only from unified storage, so the missed legacy write is invisible to API clients, but rollback to a legacy-read mode drops every write made in mode 3. The new playlist mode 3 integration tests that expect the legacy HTTP API to show k8s writes will fail or flake for the same reason.

findings.title: Background legacy writes use the caller's objects without a copy
findings.body: The legacy goroutines call Legacy.Create with the same obj pointer passed to Storage.Create (line 55), Legacy.Update with the same objInfo (line 139), and Legacy.DeleteCollection with the same listOptions (line 165). k8s create/update/delete-collection mutate those values in place (generated name, UID, resourceVersion, continue/resourceVersion on list options), and the caller may keep using them after the method returns. The goroutine therefore races with the storage layer and the client. Legacy create can also reject the object because resourceVersion/UID were already set by unified storage, or it can persist a different name than the one returned to the client. Deep-copy the inputs before the unified call (and clear server-assigned resourceVersion on the legacy copy) before handing them to the goroutine.

findings.title: Legacy update no longer writes the object stored in unified storage
findings.body: The previous Update loaded the unified object, ran objInfo.UpdatedObject once, and passed an updateWrapper so Legacy.Update received the exact object just written to unified storage. That wrapper is gone. Legacy.Update is now invoked with the original objInfo, so it loads the legacy row and re-runs UpdatedObject plus the client's preconditions against that row. Mode 3 serves reads from unified storage, so the resourceVersion on the update is the unified one and will not match legacy; a normal precondition check fails the legacy update with a conflict and the backup copy is never updated. Even if legacy ignores resourceVersion, a patch is applied to drifted legacy state instead of replacing it with the unified result, so the stores diverge. Delete has the same precondition problem: line 112 forwards the caller's DeleteOptions, including a unified-storage resourceVersion precondition, into Legacy.Delete.

findings.title: Unified NotFound skips the legacy delete
findings.body: Delete returns immediately on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound, and never starts the legacy delete. The previous implementation still deleted from legacy when unified storage returned NotFound, and only treated other errors as fatal. After a failed or cancelled legacy delete, a retry sees NotFound in unified storage (the source of truth for reads) and now leaves the legacy object in place permanently. Orphans also remain for objects that exist only in legacy. NotFound should still be returned to the client, but the async legacy delete should run so the backup store is cleaned up.

findings.title: Latencies are recorded on the wrong store's metric
findings.body: On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) and never records a storage sample, so unified-storage create failures show up as legacy failures and storage error latency is missing. Update does the same on line 129 (recordLegacyDuration for a storage error). DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine calls recordStorageDuration (line 166) with the legacy start time, so legacy delete-collection latency and errors are added to the storage histogram and the legacy series stays empty. Dashboards and any mode-promotion checks that compare legacy vs storage success will attribute outages to the wrong store and can page or block migration incorrectly.

findings.title: Successful delete metrics use the object name as the kind label
findings.body: The delete success path calls recordStorageDuration with name (the object name) as the third argument, while the error path two lines above and every other method pass options.Kind. That label is the resource kind. Every successful delete therefore emits a unique series per object name, which is unbounded cardinality on a hot write path and can exhaust Prometheus memory. Success and failure also cannot be aggregated together because they do not share the same label value, so delete success rate is not measurable.

findings.title: Legacy write failures are not logged
findings.body: The goroutines in Create (line 56), Delete (line 113), Update (line 140), and DeleteCollection (line 166) only feed the legacy error into a duration metric and otherwise discard it. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy create/update/delete/delete-collection failures. With writes now best-effort and easy to cancel, a broken legacy path produces no log line, so operators cannot tell which object diverged or why (conflict, timeout, cancelled context, validation). Log errObjectSt/err with the object name before recording the metric.

findings.title: Expected NotFound responses are logged as errors
findings.body: Get logs every Storage.Get error at Error level, including NotFound (line 71). List (line 87) and Delete (line 102) do the same, and the apierrors.IsNotFound guard that the old Delete used was removed. NotFound on get/delete is a normal client result (the playlist tests even delete twice and expect it). Those calls will flood error logs and hide real storage failures. Log NotFound at a higher verbosity, or not at all, and keep Error for unexpected failures.

findings.title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes
findings.body: Destroy closes Storage and then Legacy immediately and does not track the goroutines started by Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Those goroutines can still be inside Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection after Legacy.Destroy returns, which races with teardown and can panic or hit a closed database. Shutdown also drops the backup writes the goroutines were supposed to finish. A WaitGroup (or similar) should be added around the legacy goroutines and waited on in Destroy before calling Legacy.Destroy.

findings.title: Unit tests never check that the legacy write happens
findings.body: Mode 3 success tests register legacy mock expectations but return as soon as the unified call finishes (Create at line 65, and the same pattern in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection) and never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. The defining behavior — an asynchronous legacy write — is therefore untested, and a cancelled or skipped legacy call still passes. Legacy and unified also share one testify mock, so method names like Create cannot be attributed to a store; the "unified store fails" create case only stubs the legacy Create expectation, which the synchronous storage call consumes by accident. testify mocks are not thread-safe, so the background call can also race or panic after the test function returns.

findings.title: Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy is updated before the handler returns
findings.body: The new mode 3 cases (file at line 132, unified storage at line 191, etcd at line 287) reuse doPlaylistTests. That helper creates, updates, and deletes through the k8s client and then immediately requires the legacy /api/playlists API to match (search at line 529 and getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 returns after the unified write and only then writes legacy on another goroutine whose context is tied to the request. The legacy HTTP read therefore races the backup write and, because that context is cancelled when the request ends, will often never see the object. These new integration cases will fail or flake until the test waits for the legacy write or the dual writer detaches that work from request cancellation.
